extracted.intended_audience: journalists, copy editors and reporters (Reuters newsroom and affiliated news services)
extracted.subtask_description: A-to-Z style and usage rules for writing and editing Reuters news copy, covering wording, spelling, punctuation, capitalization, abbreviations, sensitive terminology and units/figures. Intended to guide reporters and editors on consistent, legally cautious, and audience-appropriate language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket initials after first reference when reusing
rubrics_metrics.description: Bracket initials after the first reference, e.g. The Western European Union (WEU) decided on Tuesday. In the case of foreign groups, where the word order changes in the English translation, bracket the initials, e.g. the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN). Do not bracket initials after a first reference if you are not going to use the initials again lower in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only bracket and define initials if the initials will be used subsequently; for foreign names whose word order changes on translation, include initials at first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming plurals of abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the plural of abbreviations by adding a lower-case s without an apostrophe, e.g. ICBMs not ICBM’s or ICBMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Months abbreviations in datelines and dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use full stops when abbreviating the names of months in datelines. The style is Jan, Feb, March, April, May, June, July, Aug, Sept, Oct, Nov, Dec. In tabulated lists use only the first three letters for all months, e.g. Jan, Jun, Jul. Abbreviate the names of months in text when they are used with a specific date, e.g. Jan. 19, Dec. 25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In datelines use the abbreviated form without periods; in running text abbreviate months only with specific dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalisation in abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capital letters when abbreviating capitalised words, lower case for uncapitalised phrases, e.g. ASEAN but mph, bpd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling rule for -able
rubrics_metrics.description: Words ending in a silent -e normally drop the 'e' before the -able, e.g. arguable. Words ending in -ce or -ge do not, e.g. changeable, ageing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'atomic bomb' not 'A-bomb' (except in direct quotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use atomic bomb, unless in a direct quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abortion terminology — use neutral, specific language
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless quoting someone, refer to aborted foetuses rather than unborn babies. Describe those campaigning for a woman’s right to have an abortion as abortion rights campaigners and those campaigning against abortion rights as anti-abortion campaigners. Terms such as pro-choice, pro-life and pro-abortion are open to dispute and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loaded or partisan labels; prefer descriptive phrases that identify the position rather than emotive shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABS definition (Asset-backed securities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asset-backed securities: securities collateralised by assets such as car loans and credit card receivables, which can be seized if the debtor defaults. ABS are created by the process of securitisation whereby banks pool types of loans and use them as collateral or security against a bond issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic titles capitalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise when they immediately precede a personal name, otherwise use lower case, e.g. Professor John Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept vs except
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept is to take or receive; except is to leave out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use 'access' as a verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use as a verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer alternative verbs (e.g. 'reach', 'gain access to') rather than turning 'access' into an active verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: accidentally
rubrics_metrics.description: accidentally, not accidently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: accolade
rubrics_metrics.description: accolade, not acolade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: accommodate
rubrics_metrics.description: accommodate, not accomodate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achilles' heel punctuation and capitalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Achilles’ heel, tendon — Note apostrophe and capitalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: acknowledgment, not acknowledgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: acolyte
rubrics_metrics.description: acolyte, not acolite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acre to hectare conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: To convert to hectares roughly multiply by 2 and divide by 5. To convert precisely multiply by 0.405.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid acronyms where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid if at all possible. Very few are understandable at first reference. Most are only of use to a specialised audience that has seen them several times before. Where possible replace with a noun such as the committee, the organisation, the inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use acronyms when they aid clarity and will be familiar to the audience; otherwise spell out or substitute a descriptive noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting before a title not capitalised
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalise before a title, acting Chairman and Chief Executive Paulo Georgio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity often redundant
rubrics_metrics.description: The word can often be dropped, as in sporting activity, golfing activity, leisure activity, political activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit needless 'activity' words to tighten copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor/Actress usage
rubrics_metrics.description: actor (man), actress (woman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate gendered noun if relevant; otherwise consider 'actor' as a neutral term where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute vs chronic
rubrics_metrics.description: Acute is coming to a crisis, chronic is lasting a long time or deep-seated. Be specific when writing about disease or problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague medical usage; specify condition severity and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: AD/BC usage
rubrics_metrics.description: AD Anno Domini (in the year of our Lord). Precedes the date, e.g. AD 73. But 234 BC (Before Christ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AD before date and BC after the year number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adage usage — avoid tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: A proverb or old saying. Old adage is tautologous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundant modifiers like 'old' when using 'adage'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapter vs adaptor
rubrics_metrics.description: An adapter is the person who adapts something. An adaptor is a device for connecting parts of different sizes. American style uses adapter for both.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADB definition (Asian Development Bank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asian Development Bank. A multilateral development finance institution, with headquarters in Manila, dedicated to reducing poverty in Asia and the Pacific. Owned by member countries, mostly from the region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'more or' not 'additional/in addition to'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use more or and.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'more' or 'and' instead of clumsy 'additional' or 'in addition to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives sparingly and hyphenation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sparingly. Inject colour into copy with strong verbs and facts, rather than adjectives. If you use more than two adjectives before a single noun then rewrite the sentence. Avoid adjectives that imply judgment. When using an adjective and a noun together as an adjective, hyphenate them, e.g. a blue-chip share, high-caste Hindus. When using an adjective and the past participle of a verb together adjectivally, hyphenate them, e.g. old-fashioned morality, rose-tinted spectacles. Do not hyphenate an adverb and adjective when they stand alone, e.g. the artist was well known. If the adverb and adjective are paired to form a new adjective, they are hyphenated, e.g. a well-known artist. Do not do so however if the adverb ends in -ly, e.g. a poorly planned operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit stacked adjectives; use hyphens for adjectival compounds except when the adverb ends in -ly; avoid judgmental adjectives without sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ad-lib hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated for verb, noun and adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration lowercase
rubrics_metrics.description: Always lower case, e.g. the Bush administration. See also capitalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiral — see capitalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: See capitalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: admissible, inadmissible, not admissable

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'admissions of responsibility' phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions of responsibility is officialese. Did they do it or didn't they?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain language; specify the factual admission rather than bureaucratic phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'admit' with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Use with care. If you say someone admitted something you imply that it had previously been concealed or that there is an element of guilt. Plain said is usually better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'said' or attribute to avoid implying guilt unless legally established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption reporting sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to a child’s adoptive status only when the fact is clearly significant. Use the term 'birth mother' to refer to the woman who gave birth to a child, if a distinction must be made with the woman who raised the child. 'Birth father' and 'birth parent' are also preferred style. Do not use 'real' or 'natural' to describe parents or children. Avoid loaded and dated phrases such as 'give away a child', 'give up for adoption' and 'unwanted child'. 'Adoptive' as an adjective can refer to parents or the general subject of adoption. Try to describe actions instead of creating labels such as 'adopted child' e.g. 'Hollywood actress Sharon Celebrity, who gave birth to a daughter on Friday, has two other children. She adopted Pixie, 4, and Tinkerbell, 2, during her previous marriage to actor Tim Hunk.' Be wary of cultural bias or value judgments in covering international adoptions and disputes over parental rights involving families from different cultures or socio-economic backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, non-judgmental language; prefer factual descriptions over labels and be sensitive to cross-cultural issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADR definition
rubrics_metrics.description: American Depositary Receipt. Certificates tradeable like shares that allow U.S. investors to buy stock in an overseas company while realising capital gains and dividends in dollars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: adrenaline
rubrics_metrics.description: adrenaline, not adrenalin

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance vs advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance is progress; advancement is promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance planning is a tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance planning — A tautology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundant phrasing; tighten copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs sparingly and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Like adjectives they should be used sparingly. Avoid adverbs that imply judgment, e.g. generously, harshly, and sternly. Put the adverb between the auxiliary verb and the past participle, e.g. France has already refused... not France already has refused ... However, American usage favours keeping the auxiliary verb and past participle together, with the adverb either before or after the compound verb. e.g. France has refused already... or France already has refused...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adverbs only when necessary; follow recommended positioning for clarity (between auxiliary and past participle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse vs averse
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverse is contrary, opposed or unfavourable. Averse is disinclined to or reluctant. I am averse to go camping in adverse weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct term to avoid mismeaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice vs advise
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice is the noun, advise is the verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'adviser' not 'advisor'
rubrics_metrics.description: adviser — Not advisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'aircraft' not 'aeroplane' or 'airplane'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use aircraft. Do not use the U.S. term airplane. In many cases stories need the specific type of aircraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise type (e.g. Boeing 747-400) in economic/technical contexts; consult Jane's All the World’s Aircraft for maker names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air fare and air force as two words
rubrics_metrics.description: air fare — Two words. air force — Two words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air Force One and Marine One explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Air Force One is the radio call sign of any fixed-wing aircraft used by the president of the United States. The U.S. Marine Corps is responsible for presidential helicopter support. Marine One is the radio call sign of any helicopter used by the president.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air France-KLM hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Air France-KLM — Note hyphen

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve 'airlift' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use as a synonym for fly, e.g. The injured man was airlifted to hospital. Reserve it for shuttle services, e.g. The United States airlifted 50,000 troops to the Gulf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'airlift' only for organised shuttle/transport operations, not generic flying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check airline official naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Airlines vary widely in their use of air line(s), airline(s) or airways as part of their name. Check the spelling on the company’s Web site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aircraft naming and punctuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise but do not put in quotation marks the names of aircraft, e.g. Concorde, Flogger, Tomcat. When the number designating an aircraft is preceded by a letter or letters, hyphenate, e.g. Boeing 747 but DC-10, F-111. Be specific when giving aircraft models in economic stories because there are cost differences, e.g. Boeing 747-400 not just Boeing 747. Use makers’ names in the form given in Jane’s All the World’s Aircraft, e.g. MiG-21. Give numerals for aircraft speeds, e.g. Mach 1 not Mach one. Aircraft names use a hyphen when changing from letters to figures, no hyphen when adding a letter to figures, eg F-15 Eagle/747B, but Airbus 3000 is an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow hyphenation and capitalization rules for clarity and accuracy; be precise about models in business/economic reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air lift vs airlift distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: airlift — Do not use as a synonym for fly; reserve for shuttle services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Airlines and air raid/air strike two-word rules
rubrics_metrics.description: air raid — Two words. air strike — Two words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'alleged' and sourcing carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. Do not report allegations without saying who made them. Use of the word alleged before a defamatory statement does not provide immunity against an action for libel. Do not use allegedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always attribute allegations and avoid relying on' alleged' as a blanket legal shield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Al Jazeera styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Al Jazeera — Qatar television station. Use upper case A and no hyphen since this is how the broadcaster describes itself in English. Refer to as an Arab news channel broadcasting in Arabic and in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: al Qaeda contextual precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Now the term al Qaeda is used by different people to mean different things. When authorities speak about an 'al Qaeda plot', we should try to pin down whether they mean it was ordered and directed by 'core al Qaeda' or generally inspired by the anti-Western ideology of bin Laden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about which network, cell or inspiration is meant when using 'al Qaeda'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Albino plural and related spellings
rubrics_metrics.description: albino, albinos

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'alfresco' meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use in the open air, or outdoors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alias usage restricted to false name
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers only to assumption of a false name, not an entire false identity or profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: All right not 'alright'
rubrics_metrics.description: all right — Not alright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'backlash' as cliché
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. It is more effective to describe what happened and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'backlash' with specific description of reactions and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backwardation definition in commodity markets
rubrics_metrics.description: In commodity markets, backwardation is a situation where the cash or near delivery price rises above the price for forward delivery. The forward price is normally higher than the cash price to reflect the added costs of storage and insurance for stocks deliverable at a later date. The opposite of backwardation is contango.

rubrics_metrics.name: Billion usage in Reuters services
rubrics_metrics.description: In Reuters services billion means one thousand million. The word billion must be spelled out, although it can be abbreviated to bln if necessary in headlines. Always use figures before million and billion, e.g. 2 billion, 3 million. When reporting a range of figures, use the style 1.2 billion to 1.4 billion not 1.2-1.4 billion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'bln' in headlines only where space requires; ensure numeric formatting in ranges uses 'to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophes: possessive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the apostrophe according to the following rules, unless to do so would lead to a word that looked or sounded very strange. Singular words and plural words not ending in s form the possessive by adding ‘s, e.g. Boeing’s new airliner, the children’s books. Plural words already ending in s form the possessive by adding the apostrophe alone, e.g. the soldiers’ weapons. There is usually no problem about using the apostrophe with words ending in s. the class’s performance, the princesses’ return, Shultz’s car are all acceptable because they can be pronounced easily. Some words would look or sound so odd, e.g. Paris’s reputation, Tunis’s main prison or Woolworths’s results that it best to write your way out of trouble. Recast such phrases, e.g. the son of the Dukasises, the reputation of Paris, the main prison in Tunis and results from Woolworths. Companies which end in s like Qantas or Optus might also appear ugly with the ‘s possessive. The best option is to avoid if possible. Reuters does not take an apostrophe, the only exception being in connection with the founder’s name, e.g. Reuter’s birthplace in Kassel. Note that it’s is a contraction of it is. The possessive form of it is its. Do not use an apostrophe in for example the 1990s or abbreviations such as NCOs. Joint possession: use the possessive form only after the last word if ownership is joint, e.g. Fred and Sylvia's apartment, but the possessive of both words if the objects and individually owned, e.g. Fred's And Sylvia's books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid awkward possessives by recasting; follow rules for joint possession and avoid apostrophes in decades and common abbreviations; remember 'its' is possessive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerals for ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Use numerals for all ages, e.g. the 6-year-old girl, the 9-year-old boy. The 66-year-old president or an 18-year-old youth are fine. Avoid the 66-year-old Smith, which suggests he is being distinguished from another, 65-year-old Smith; said instead, in a simple way, Smith, who is 66, or just Smith, 66.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise age constructions; avoid awkward hyphenated noun identifiers when they create ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'aged' and 'elderly' as vague
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid, because the terms are always relative. In some societies a 50-year-old is already aged. In others a sprightly 90-year-old who has just written a novel or run a marathon would object to being called aged or elderly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise ages or descriptors rather than blanket labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: American spelling guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy originating in the Americas should follow North American spelling conventions... Copy originating elsewhere should follow British spelling norms. At all times stick to official spellings for American names and titles, such as U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Watch out for regional words that non-English language services and clients will find difficult to understand and translate. In American sports coverage, use American terms and spellings e.g. center, maneuver, defense, offense, ballclub, postseason, preseason, lineman, line up, halfback, doubleheader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent regional spelling based on story origin; adhere to official names and local terminology where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Believed phrasing: source all beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs must be sourced. Do not write, 'John Smith was believed to have been killed in an ambush.' Say who believes and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute beliefs and the basis for them to avoid vague or potentially libelous statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and sensitive descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid adjectives that imply judgment and use more specific descriptions rather than labels that may be contested by different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, describe actions or facts rather than applying loaded adjectives.
